newsitem.title: CHINA: China vows good treatment for Gore during visit.
newsitem.headline: China vows good treatment for Gore during visit.

text.p: Chinese Premier Li Peng on Friday waved aside allegations that Beijing had tried to fund politicians in the United States and vowed to treat U.S. Vice President Al Gore well when he visits China later this month.

China did not meddle in other nations' concerns, Li told reporters after being asked to comment on reports that Beijing attempted to make illegal donations to U.S. Democratic Party politicians during the 1996 U.S. presidential election campaign.
"The Chinese government itself would not use any means to interfere or influence any other country's internal affairs," Li said.

The Washington Post reported last Sunday that the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions from foreign corporations.
U.S. investigators had found what officials called conclusive evidence that Chinese government funds were funnelled into the United States in 1996, the newspaper said.

The allegations, which prompted a senior Chinese foreign ministry official to make serious representations to the U.S. charge d'affairs in Beijing, were the latest strain in the sensitive Sino-U.S. relationship.

Cross-Pacific ties have long been buffeted by disputes over issues ranging from human rights to Taiwan to trade, but both sides have made great efforts in recent months to put their relations on more stable footing.
Beijing would take good care of U.S. Vice President Gore when he visited China later this month, Premier Li said.
"Vice President Al Gore... will receive very good treatment," he said.

The arrival of Gore, the most senior American to visit China in eight years, would pave the way for an exchange of visits between U.S. President Bill Clinton and his Chinese counterpart Jiang Zemin, Li said.
Jiang is expected to set the seal on the recent Sino-U.S. rapprochement with a visit the United States later this year.
China wanted to overcome its differences with the United States, Li said.
"We have some disagreements but hope to reduce confrontation and expand cooperation in order to develop our relationship along a normal track," Li said.
"To maintain the healthy and stable development of the Sino-U.S. relationship will be in the interests of world peace and stability," Li said.
